Map abstract

This resource map showcases copper deposits and their density throughout Arizona. This foundational map aims to show how, in relation to the other maps, the location of the copper deposits in Arizona has influenced other data like demographics, environmental health, and economic inequality. The digital version of the map helps display the number of copper mines that began operation per year, with there being a significant increase from around 1910-1920—coinciding with America’s adoption of electricity. Copper is needed for electrical purposes due to its conductivity properties, so the increase in demand would cause an increase in mines. 70 million years ago, magma cooled within the Earth’s crust and expelled fluids which formed copper deposits below the surface.¹ These processes explain how geology millions of years ago influenced where copper mines are today, and by extension, the data of all of the other maps. All of this resource data was sourced from the Mineral Reosources Data Catalog by the U.S. Geological Survey.²

1. King Copper. (2017). Arizona Geological Survey - AZGS. https://azgs.arizona.edu/mineral-resources/mining-arizona/king-copper.
2. Mrdata.Usgs.Gov. n.d. “Mineral Resources Data System: By Commodity.” Accessed November 4, 2026. https://mrdata.usgs.gov/mrds/map-commodity.html.

Source

U.S. Geological Survey. Mineral Resources Data System (MRDS), Arizona (FIPS 04), filtered to records listing copper as a commodity (5,244 sites). mrdata.usgs.gov/mrds. The shaded-relief underlay is the USGS “State of Arizona” 1:500,000 relief map, georeferenced to this map and clipped to the state outline (also traced from that map). Rivers and ranges are hand-simplified for context; place names and the formation timeline follow the Arizona Geological Survey’s “King Copper.”
